tasks.explanation: Records and requirements are compared before field practice is observed, so the observation tests the real gaps. Corrections are owned and tracked, and the committee receives the full picture.

tasks.prompt: Order a work order management review for collection maintenance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater collection scenario for Class 3 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, Ontario Regulation 129/04 requirements where they apply, and standard collection system practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: the backlog has grown to 400 open work orders and supervisors suspect duplicates, stale priorities, and completed work left open.

cards.label: Brief the crews and supervisors on the cleaned backlog and the new scheduling and closing discipline
Set the scheduling rules so high risk work is assigned first and routine work is bundled by area
Reprioritize the verified backlog using the criticality of the asset and the risk the defect carries
Report backlog size, age, and completion rate monthly until the backlog reaches the target level
Sample work orders in each group and verify them against field reality, closing completed work and merging true duplicates
Extract the backlog and analyse it by age, priority, asset, and work type to find where it is concentrated

tasks.explanation: The backlog is analysed and verified before it is reprioritized, because scheduling fiction helps no one. Monthly reporting continues until the backlog is actually at target, not just tidier.

tasks.prompt: Order an operations budget variance review and corrective action cycle.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater collection scenario for Class 3 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, Ontario Regulation 129/04 requirements where they apply, and standard collection system practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: mid year results show chemical, overtime, and contractor costs over budget while cleaning completion is behind plan.

cards.label: Separate the variances caused by price, by volume of work, and by emergency events that were not in the plan
Identify the lines where spending can be corrected without cutting required compliance or safety work
Build the corrective actions, such as rescheduling discretionary work or bringing contracted work in house where crews have capacity
Present the variance analysis and the corrective actions to management for approval
Confirm the actual costs and the work delivered for each budget line from the financial and work order records
Track the corrected lines monthly and report whether the year end forecast returns to budget

tasks.explanation: Costs are matched with work actually delivered before variances are explained. Price, volume, and emergency causes need different corrections, and compliance work is protected explicitly.

tasks.prompt: Order the preparation for a Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks inspection of the collection system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater collection scenario for Class 3 study. Conditions are as stated in the configuration, and all work follows site procedures, Ontario Regulation 129/04 requirements where they apply, and standard collection system practice.
tasks.configuration: Scope: an inspection of the Class 3 collection system and its records has been scheduled with two weeks notice.

cards.label: Host the inspection and log the inspector questions, the records provided, and any findings in the inspection file
Confirm the inspection scope and the records the inspector has requested and assign the staff who will host and support the visit
Assemble the requested records, including licences, overall responsible operator designations, overflow records, and training files, and check them for completeness
Inspect the stations and current work sites the inspector is likely to visit and correct housekeeping or record gaps found
Brief the hosting staff on answering accurately, providing records as requested, and recording every request and finding
Respond to the inspection report with the corrective actions and dates through the required channel and track them in the CMOM file

tasks.explanation: Scope and records come first, and the hosting sites are checked honestly before the visit. A complete inspection log makes the response to the report accurate and complete.

tasks.prompt: A Class 3 operator compares two basins after main lining: Basin A night flow fell by half, Basin B night flow did not change.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basins of similar size and pipe age, both lined in the same season. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Basin A minimum night flow fell from 18 L/s to 9 L/s after lining and stayed low for three dry months.
Basin B minimum night flow stayed at 17 L/s after lining over the same three dry months.
Basin B has many shallow manholes in a creek floodplain, Basin A manholes are on high ground.
Groundwater levels were high in both basins during the whole comparison period.
CCTV after lining shows no joint infiltration in the mains of either basin.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Basin A flows fell because residents used less water at night
Basin B lining failed and its mains still leak at every joint
Groundwater was low in Basin B so no infiltration could occur
Basin B infiltration is entering mainly through manholes and laterals, not through the lined mains

inference.explanation: Both mains are tight on CCTV, yet only Basin A improved, so Basin B water must enter outside the mains. Floodplain manholes fit that path, and high groundwater rules out the low groundwater distractor. Night use does not halve after lining by chance in one basin only.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Re-lining Basin B mains a second time
A household water use survey in Basin A
Manhole inspection and flow isolation in Basin B, checking floodplain manholes and lateral connections at night

nextClue.explanation: Isolating where Basin B night flow enters, at manholes and laterals, tests the only path left after the mains proved tight.

clueText.nc-a: Basin B mains already proved tight on CCTV, so a second lining treats a path that is not leaking.
clueText.nc-b: Home use was similar in both basins, so a survey cannot explain why only one basin improved.
clueText.nc-c: Floodplain manholes in Basin B show infiltration at frame seals and two laterals run clear water at 3 a.m.

tasks.prompt: Night flow in a basin stays high after every main joint is sealed, and the operator must find the remaining source.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin after a joint sealing program. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Dry weather minimum night flow is 14 L/s in a basin where expected sanitary night flow is about 5 L/s.
Post sealing CCTV shows all main joints dry during a high groundwater week.
Step isolation at night shows one 300 m reach contributes 8 of the 9 extra L/s.
That reach has 22 laterals and no manholes below the water table.
Smoke testing on that reach finds three laterals smoking at cleanouts with cracked caps.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Water use in the basin is simply higher than the estimate
Cracked lateral cleanouts and defective laterals on one reach are the dominant remaining infiltration source
The treatment plant is returning flow into the basin at night
The main joints are still leaking despite the dry CCTV

inference.explanation: Isolation puts almost all extra flow in one reach, the mains there are dry on camera, and smoke testing finds open lateral defects on that reach. A plant return would not isolate to one reach, and an estimate error would not produce cracked cleanouts smoking.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Another round of main joint sealing across the whole basin
Lateral camera inspections on the isolated reach, starting at the three smoking cleanouts
A plant effluent flow audit

nextClue.explanation: Cameras in the laterals of the isolated reach confirm which private side defects carry the water the step test located.

clueText.nc-a: The mains already test dry, so more main sealing repeats work on a tight asset.
clueText.nc-b: Lateral cameras show groundwater entering at cracked joints in five laterals on the isolated reach.
clueText.nc-c: No return path from the plant to this basin exists in the records, and flow isolated to one reach.

tasks.prompt: A city must decide whether high wet weather flow in Basin C is groundwater infiltration or direct inflow before funding a program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario Basin C with flow and rain records for 12 storms. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Basin C flow rises within 20 minutes of rain starting and falls within 2 hours of rain ending, in all 12 storms.
Dry weather night flow in Basin C is normal for its population in both wet and dry seasons.
Basin size and rainfall are similar to Basin D, where flow rises slowly and stays high for two days after rain.
Roof leader disconnection records show many Basin C homes still connect roof leaders to the sanitary sewer.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Basin C response is groundwater infiltration through pipe joints
Basin C flow meters drift high only during rain
Basin C response is direct inflow from connected sources such as roof leaders, not groundwater infiltration
Basin D is the inflow basin and Basin C is the infiltration basin

inference.explanation: A rise in minutes and recovery in hours is the signature of direct inflow, and normal dry night flow rules out a large groundwater component. Basin D shows the slow, long infiltration pattern instead, and connected roof leaders supply the direct path.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A groundwater well drilling program around Basin C
Flow meter recalibration only, with no source survey
Roof leader and foundation drain survey in Basin C, paired with storm event flow timing

nextClue.explanation: Surveying the direct connections tests the fast response path the timing data identified.

clueText.nc-a: Dry night flow is already normal, so groundwater is not the driver a well program would chase.
clueText.nc-b: Two independent meters agree during storms, so drift does not explain the pattern.
clueText.nc-c: The survey finds most sampled homes connect roof leaders, and disconnecting a test block cuts its storm peak by a third.

tasks.prompt: After a lateral lining program, a supervisor reviews whether private side work actually reduced infiltration in the target basin.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin, 180 laterals lined, with two matched control basins. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Minimum night flow in the target basin fell 40 percent after lining and stayed down through one full high groundwater season.
Two similar unlined control basins showed no night flow change over the same season.
Rainfall and groundwater levels were near average in both the before and after seasons.
Main flows upstream of the basin did not change, so no flow was diverted elsewhere.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Residents reduced night water use by 40 percent in one year
The lateral lining caused the reduction, because the matched controls rule out season and weather effects
Flow was diverted upstream so the basin only appears improved
The reduction was caused by a dry season with low groundwater

inference.explanation: Controls with the same weather did not change, groundwater was near average, and no diversion occurred, leaving the lining as the difference. A dry season is contradicted by the groundwater record.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A resident water use survey as the sole follow up
A second season of night flow monitoring in target and control basins to confirm the gain holds
Immediate lining of the control basins with no further monitoring

nextClue.explanation: Confirming the gain holds for a second season, against controls, is the audit step before the result is claimed program wide.

clueText.nc-a: Use surveys cannot explain a change that controls with similar homes did not show.
clueText.nc-b: Second season data show the target basin still 35 percent below baseline while controls remain at baseline.
clueText.nc-c: Lining controls now would destroy the comparison that proves the program works.

tasks.prompt: Flow monitors in two sub-basins disagree about which area drives infiltration, and the Class 3 operator must resolve it.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario twin sub-basins with temporary meters for one spring. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Sub-basin North night flow per kilometre of sewer is three times the South value in dry weather.
Both sub-basins have the same pipe material, age, and average depth.
North sewers run below a creek water level for most of their length, South sewers run above it.
Dye testing shows no cross connection between the sub-basins.
When North is isolated at its outlet at night, downstream flow falls by the full North amount.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The North meter over reads by a factor of three
North residents use three times more water at night than South residents
Submerged North sewers below creek level take in groundwater through defects, driving the higher rate
South flow leaks out of its sewers so its rate only looks low

inference.explanation: Same pipe and age remove material as the cause, isolation confirms the North volume is real, and dye rules out cross flow. Submergence below creek level is the remaining difference that explains a threefold rate.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: CCTV and joint testing in the submerged North reaches during high creek levels
A night water use survey in North homes
Meter replacement in South only

nextClue.explanation: Inspecting the submerged reaches while creek levels are high looks for entry at the defects the rate analysis points to.

clueText.nc-a: CCTV in the submerged reaches shows steady joint infiltration at multiple joints below creek level.
clueText.nc-b: Isolation already proved the volume is real sewage plus groundwater, not a use pattern artifact.
clueText.nc-c: The South meter was verified by the isolation balance, so replacing it does not address North.

tasks.prompt: A supervisor must choose between manhole rehabilitation and main lining for the next capital year in an old basin.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin condition and flow data assembled for capital planning. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Manhole inspection grades 60 percent of basin manholes as poor, with infiltration visible at frames and benches.
CCTV grades most mains as fair, with infiltration at only a few joints.
Night flow isolation shows flow steps up sharply at two floodplain manhole clusters.
A pilot that sealed 20 manholes in one cluster cut that cluster night flow contribution by 70 percent.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Neither project is justified because CCTV shows the system is fair overall
Main lining should be funded first because mains are longer than manholes
The pilot result was luck and should be ignored in planning
Manhole rehabilitation should be funded first, because manholes are the measured dominant entry path

inference.explanation: Inspections, isolation steps, and a measured pilot all point to manholes, while mains show only a few leaking joints. Length alone is not evidence, and an overall fair grade hides the measured manhole losses.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Full manhole condition scoring with infiltration rated per manhole, to rank the rehabilitation list
Deferring all work until a bypass occurs
A main lining design for the whole basin

nextClue.explanation: Scoring every manhole by infiltration ranks the work the pilot already proved effective.

clueText.nc-a: Scoring confirms the floodplain clusters carry most of the rated infiltration, matching the isolation steps.
clueText.nc-b: A basin wide lining design spends on mains that CCTV shows are mostly tight.
clueText.nc-c: Waiting for a bypass ignores measured losses and the pilot proof already in hand.

tasks.prompt: An inflow investigation finds sanitary flow spikes only on the first day of heavy rain after long dry periods.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin with event records over two years. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Spikes occur on the first heavy rain after dry spells of two weeks or more, not on later rainy days.
Catch basin cross connection checks in the basin find several storm grates tied into the sanitary sewer.
After those cross connections are removed, the first rain spike falls by half in a matched test storm.
Dry weather flows and groundwater levels show no matching spike pattern.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Pump stations store flow and release it on rainy days
First rains wash roof sediment that blocks and then clears sewers
Direct storm cross connections, filling and flushing on first rains, cause the first day spikes
Groundwater infiltration rises and falls within a single day

inference.explanation: Groundwater cannot rise and fall in a day and shows no matching pattern, while removing cross connections halved the spike in a matched storm. That direct test confirms the storm tie ins as a real cause.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A groundwater monitoring well network
Pump station storage logs review only
A basin wide cross connection survey using dye at storm grates during dry weather

nextClue.explanation: Dye surveying every storm grate finds the remaining tie ins the partial removal proved are driving the spikes.

clueText.nc-a: Dry weather and groundwater records already show no matching pattern for wells to explain.
clueText.nc-b: Station logs show normal operation on spike days, so storage release is not the pattern.
clueText.nc-c: The survey finds four more tied grates, and removing them cuts the next first rain spike again.

tasks.prompt: A Class 3 audit compares claimed infiltration reduction from a grouting program against flow records.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario grouting program with contractor claims and city flow records. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: The contractor claims a 50 percent infiltration reduction based on grout volume used.
City night flow records for the grouted basin show only a 5 percent reduction over the same period.
A control basin with no grouting shows a 4 percent reduction over the same period.
Post grouting CCTV in a sample reach shows several joints still weeping.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The control basin reduction proves grouting worked city wide
The city flow meters must be wrong because grout volume proves success
The program delivered little real reduction, and grout volume is not a valid measure of flow removed
Weeping joints on CCTV are normal after successful grouting

inference.explanation: City records and a nearly equal control change show the basin barely moved, and sample joints still weep. Grout volume measures material placed, not water stopped, and the control comparison removes weather as an excuse.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Joint by joint post grouting CCTV with infiltration rated before and after, on a random sample
Ordering double grout volume in the same reaches
Accepting the contractor claim and closing the audit

nextClue.explanation: A random before and after camera sample measures actual water stopped, which is what the claim must be judged on.

clueText.nc-a: The sample shows most grouted joints still weep, matching the small flow change in city records.
clueText.nc-b: Closing the audit would accept a claim the flow records already contradict.
clueText.nc-c: More grout volume repeats the same invalid measure without locating the leaking joints.

tasks.prompt: Foundation drains are suspected in a new subdivision where sanitary flows surge in every moderate rain.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario subdivision, five years old, with PVC sewers in good condition. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Sewer CCTV shows new PVC pipe with tight joints and no visible infiltration in dry weather.
Flows surge within an hour of rain and return to normal the same day.
Building records show foundation drains were connected to sanitary laterals on one street by a builder error.
On that street only, disconnecting test homes cuts the surge at the downstream meter in a matched rain.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The surge is normal diurnal flow that only looks rain related
The new PVC mains leak groundwater at every joint
All subdivision homes have sump pumps discharging to sanitary
Connected foundation drains on one street are the surge source, proven by the disconnection test

inference.explanation: Tight dry CCTV rules out joint infiltration, timing is inflow fast, and the matched disconnection test on the one street with the builder error cut the surge. A subdivision wide sump cause would not respond to one street of disconnections.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Main joint grouting across the subdivision
Lot by lot foundation drain connection survey across the subdivision, using the builder records as the starting list
A diurnal flow study with no connection survey

nextClue.explanation: Surveying every lot finds any remaining connected drains beyond the test street.

clueText.nc-a: Dry CCTV already shows tight joints, so grouting treats a path that is not leaking.
clueText.nc-b: The survey finds the error limited to two streets, and full disconnection removes most of the surge.
clueText.nc-c: Diurnal flow does not surge within an hour of rain, so timing already separates the two.

tasks.prompt: A basin shows high infiltration only in spring, and two competing explanations must be separated before design.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin with seasonal flow, groundwater, and river records. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Spring night flows are double winter values in the basin every year.
Groundwater wells and the adjacent river both peak in spring, matching the flow pattern.
A paired basin on high ground away from the river shows no spring rise.
Dye and CCTV in a dry spring week show no direct storm connections in the basin.
Smoke testing finds no major defects above the seasonal water table.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Spring snowmelt enters through manhole covers across the basin
Spring rain inflow through roof leaders drives the rise
Seasonal high groundwater and river levels drive infiltration through defects below the spring water table
Residents use more water in spring for cleaning

inference.explanation: The high ground paired basin removes weather alone as the cause, dry week testing removes direct connections, and the flow peak matches groundwater and river peaks. Defects below the spring table are the path left standing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: CCTV and joint testing timed to the spring high water period in the low reaches
A roof leader disconnection campaign as the first step
A spring water use survey

nextClue.explanation: Inspecting low reaches at high water catches infiltration active, which dry season inspection would miss.

clueText.nc-a: Spring CCTV shows clear water entering at joints and two manholes in the low reaches, dry in winter runs.
clueText.nc-b: Direct connections were already ruled out by dye and CCTV in a dry spring week.
clueText.nc-c: Night flows double, and household cleaning does not double night sanitary flow.

tasks.prompt: A city must defend its overflow response to a regulator after a bypass where the overall responsible operator was off site.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario bypass response review under Ontario Regulation 129/04 overall responsible operator duties. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: The bypass was detected by alarms, reported within the required window, and sampled as required.
The designated operator in charge attended, directed containment, and logged decisions through the event.
The overall responsible operator was notified promptly, reviewed actions by phone, and attended the next morning review.
No step in the response record is missing, late, or unsigned.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Any bypass with the overall responsible operator off site is automatically a violation
Sampling during a bypass is never required
The response met the duty structure, because the operator in charge acted on site while the overall responsible operator supervised and reviewed
Alarms alone satisfy the response duties with no attendance needed

inference.explanation: The record shows each duty performed by the correct role: detection, reporting, sampling, on site direction by the operator in charge, and supervision by the overall responsible operator. Physical presence of one named person at every minute is not what the completed record faults.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Rewriting the logs to show the overall responsible operator on site
Preparing an apology for an automatic violation
Filing the complete response record, with the alarm, sampling, and decision logs attached

nextClue.explanation: Filing the true complete record is the defensible close to a compliant response.

clueText.nc-a: No violation is established by a record that shows every duty performed.
clueText.nc-b: Rewriting logs would falsify a record that is already complete and true.
clueText.nc-c: The filed record matches recorder and sampling data at every timestamp.

tasks.prompt: An operator must tell whether a sudden night flow jump in one basin is a new infiltration source or a meter fault.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin with a step change in recorded night flow. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Recorded night flow jumped from 10 L/s to 16 L/s in one day and stayed at the new level.
A portable meter installed beside the permanent meter for a week reads 10 L/s while the permanent meter reads 16 L/s.
Upstream manhole depth checks at night match the portable meter value.
No rain, construction, or new connections occurred in the basin that week.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Groundwater rose suddenly with no rain
The permanent meter is faulty, because two independent checks agree with the original flow
A new subdivision connected without records that week
A new infiltration source added 6 L/s in one day

inference.explanation: A side by side portable meter and depth checks both read the original value, so the water is not there. A real 6 L/s source appearing in one dry day with no construction is not supported by any observation.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A basin wide CCTV infiltration survey
A new connection records search only
Permanent meter calibration check and replacement, then a week of comparison against the portable meter

nextClue.explanation: Calibrating and comparing the permanent meter closes the fault the paired readings identified.

clueText.nc-a: A CCTV survey would chase water that paired meters show is not entering the basin.
clueText.nc-b: Records already show no new connections that week, so a search cannot explain a phantom step.
clueText.nc-c: Calibration finds a drifted sensor, and after replacement both meters agree at about 10 L/s.

tasks.prompt: A city lines the worst basin first, but system wet weather peaks barely fall, and the Class 3 operator must explain why.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario system with basin level wet weather data. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: The lined basin contributed only 10 percent of the system wet weather peak before lining.
Two unlined basins together contribute 60 percent of the system peak.
Lining cut the target basin wet weather flow by half, as designed.
System peak fell by about 5 percent, matching the target basin share times its reduction.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The lining failed because the system peak did not fall by half
System meters were moved during the project, hiding the gain
The program worked locally but the basin was too small a share of the system peak to move the total much
Flow from the lined basin was diverted into the other basins

inference.explanation: The arithmetic matches: half of a 10 percent share is a 5 percent system gain, and the basin itself halved as designed. No diversion or meter move is stated, and local success is directly measured.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Declaring the lining method ineffective system wide
Re-lining the same basin to chase a bigger system gain
Re-ranking remaining basins by share of system peak before selecting the next lining project

nextClue.explanation: Ranking by peak share directs the next project where the system benefit is largest.

clueText.nc-a: The basin already halved its flow, so re-lining it cannot yield another large gain.
clueText.nc-b: The method halved the treated basin, so the method is effective where the share is large.
clueText.nc-c: The ranking puts the two large share basins first, and their combined share is six times the lined basin.

tasks.prompt: Private side inflow is suspected after public side work in a basin shows no wet weather improvement.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario basin after main lining and manhole sealing. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Public mains were lined and manholes sealed, and dry night flow fell as expected.
Wet weather peaks in the basin did not fall after the public side work.
Flow rises and falls with rain within hours, while dry flow stays low.
A test block where homeowners disconnected downspouts showed a clear wet weather peak reduction in matched storms.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Remaining wet weather flow is private side inflow, proven by the downspout test block response
The test block result was caused by lower rainfall on that block
The lining failed and wet flow still enters the mains
Wet weather peaks come from groundwater that public work cannot affect

inference.explanation: Dry flow fell, so the public work held, and the fast rain response is inflow timing, not groundwater. The matched storm test block isolates private disconnection as the lever that moves the peak.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A groundwater lowering study
A second public main lining pass
A private side inflow program design, starting with downspout and foundation drain surveys basin wide

nextClue.explanation: Surveying private connections sizes the program the test block proved will move the peak.

clueText.nc-a: Dry flow already fell after lining, so the mains are not the remaining path.
clueText.nc-b: Groundwater responds over days, not within hours of rain starting and stopping.
clueText.nc-c: Surveys find widespread connected downspouts, matching the fast rise and fall timing.

tasks.prompt: Two flow meters on the same trunk read very differently during storms, and a supervisor must decide which record to trust for design.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario trunk sewer with two meters 800 m apart and no branches between them. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Dry weather flows at both meters agree within 3 percent.
During storms the downstream meter reads 30 percent higher than the upstream meter.
There are no branches, laterals of size, or storage structures between the meters.
A dye travel test shows no inflow entry points between the meters, and manhole checks find covers sealed.
The downstream meter sits just below a drop where storm flow is highly turbulent.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Sewage is created between the meters during storms
Storm inflow enters between the meters through hidden connections
The downstream meter over reads in turbulent storm flow, so the upstream record should be used for design
The upstream meter under reads in all conditions

inference.explanation: Dry agreement rules out a general upstream fault, and dye plus manhole checks rule out entry between the meters on a branchless reach. Turbulence at the downstream drop is the remaining explanation for storm only divergence.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A hidden connection excavation program between the meters
A storm event check with a portable meter in a calm section near the downstream site
Discarding both records and designing with no flow data

nextClue.explanation: A portable meter in calm water tests the turbulence explanation directly during a storm.

clueText.nc-a: Dye and cover checks already found no entry points for excavation to find.
clueText.nc-b: The portable meter in the calm section agrees with the upstream meter during the storm.
clueText.nc-c: The upstream record is verified, so design data exists and need not be discarded.

tasks.prompt: A rehabilitation audit finds infiltration returning two years after joint grouting in one basin but not in a neighbouring basin grouted the same year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario two basins grouted in the same contract year. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Basin E night flow fell after grouting and returned to baseline within two years.
Basin F night flow fell after grouting and remains low after five years.
Basin E sewers carry a high silt load and are jetted four times a year, Basin F sewers are jetted once a year.
CCTV in Basin E shows grout missing at joints in the jetted reaches, intact in a reach that is not jetted.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Basin F flows stayed low because its residents left the area
Frequent high pressure jetting in Basin E is stripping the grout, causing the early failure
Groundwater is higher in Basin E so grout cannot hold there
The grout product was defective only in Basin E

inference.explanation: Same year and program remove product batch as a basin specific cause, and grout survives in the one Basin E reach that is not jetted while it is missing where jetting is frequent. That within basin contrast isolates jetting as the difference.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A population survey in Basin F
Regrouting Basin E at double volume with no cleaning change
A jetting pressure and nozzle review for Basin E, plus a trial reach cleaned at reduced pressure with grout checked after

nextClue.explanation: Testing reduced pressure cleaning on a trial reach checks whether the grout survives gentler cleaning.

clueText.nc-a: Regrouting without changing cleaning repeats the stripping cycle the evidence shows.
clueText.nc-b: Basin F flows are night infiltration flows, not a population artifact, and its grout is intact.
clueText.nc-c: After one year the trial reach grout is intact and night flow there stays low.

tasks.prompt: Rainfall dependent inflow is quantified for design: a supervisor must decide which basin drives the trunk surcharge.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario trunk serving Basins G and H with matched storm records. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Per hectare wet weather peaking is similar in G and H for small storms.
In large storms, Basin H flow per hectare is double Basin G and lasts twice as long.
Basin H has combined sewer remnants and many area drains connected, Basin G is fully separated.
Trunk surcharge timing matches Basin H hydrograph peaks, not Basin G peaks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Both basins contribute equally in all storms
Basin H, with its connected area drains, dominates large storm response and drives the surcharge
Basin G drives the surcharge because it is larger in area
The trunk itself generates the extra storm flow

inference.explanation: Small storm similarity rules out a constant difference, while large storm doubling, longer duration, connected drains, and surcharge timing all point to H. Area alone does not explain timing that matches H peaks.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Basin H area drain disconnection scoping, with storm monitoring to verify peak reduction
Basin G separation upgrades as the first project
Trunk upsizing with no basin source work

nextClue.explanation: Scoping disconnection in H targets the basin whose hydrograph matches the surcharge.

clueText.nc-a: Scoping finds dozens of connected area drains in H concentrated in the old combined area.
clueText.nc-b: G is already fully separated, so upgrades there do not address the matched H timing.
clueText.nc-c: Upsizing alone ignores a source reduction the timing data supports.

tasks.prompt: A lift station runs almost continuously after rain but returns to normal cycling in dry weather.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lift station with run time and rainfall records. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Pump run hours triple on rain days and return to normal within a day after rain ends.
Dry weather run hours and wet well levels are normal for the station age and catchment.
Pump drawdown tests in dry weather meet the rated capacity.
Catchment CCTV shows tight mains, but many manholes sit in a flooded low area during rain.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Both pumps have lost capacity and need replacement
The wet well has shrunk due to grit buildup
A pump check valve leaks back continuously
Rainfall inflow through low area manhole covers and frames is driving the extra pump run time

inference.explanation: Pumps meet rated capacity on drawdown tests, and a check valve leak or lost capacity would raise dry run hours too. The rain only pattern with flooded low manholes points to inflow at the covers.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Manhole cover and frame inspection in the low area, with sealed covers trialled on the worst group
Wet well grit removal as the sole action
Pump replacement procurement

nextClue.explanation: Trialling sealed covers on flooded manholes tests the inflow path the rain pattern identified.

clueText.nc-a: After sealing the trial group, run hours on a matched rain day fall by a third.
clueText.nc-b: Drawdown tests already prove rated capacity, so replacement is not supported.
clueText.nc-c: Grit would affect dry cycling as well, which is normal.

tasks.prompt: One pump at a duplex station trips on overload every few days while its twin runs normally on the same wet well.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario duplex lift station, pumps alternating duty. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: Pump 2 trips on overload, Pump 1 never trips while handling the same flows.
Swapping the starter buckets between pumps moves the trip with Pump 2, not with the starter.
Pump 2 amp draw is high from the start of each run and its discharge flow is low.
Removing Pump 2 finds a rag mass wound tight in its impeller.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The starter for Pump 2 is faulty and trips it
Station voltage sags trip the larger pump only
A rag obstruction in Pump 2 impeller causes its high amps, low flow, and overload trips
Wet well grease is overloading both pumps equally

inference.explanation: The trip follows the pump when starters are swapped, ruling out the starter, and the twin runs fine on the same well, ruling out station wide causes. High amps with low flow and a rag mass found in the impeller complete the case.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: A ragging watch, amp trending on both pumps with an alarm on rising draw at normal flow
Starter replacement for Pump 2
A station voltage study

nextClue.explanation: Amp trending catches the next ragging event early, which the diagnosis shows is the recurring risk.

clueText.nc-a: Amp trend alarms two weeks later as Pump 1 draw rises, and a small rag is cleared before any trip.
clueText.nc-b: The swap test already cleared the starter, so replacing it repeats a ruled out cause.
clueText.nc-c: Both pumps share the station supply, and only one tripped, so voltage does not fit.

tasks.prompt: A lift station high level alarm repeats at the same time each morning, with no pump fault found.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario lift station serving a catchment with a large institution. Observations are as stated.

evidence.label: High level alarms occur between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. on weekdays only.
Both pumps pass drawdown and capacity tests and alternate normally.
Flow records show a sharp one hour inflow surge on weekday mornings, absent on weekends.
A boarding school in the catchment starts showers and laundry at 6 a.m. on weekdays.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A weekday morning inflow surge from the institution exceeds short term station capacity and causes the alarms
Infiltration rises every weekday morning and falls on weekends
One pump fails only in the morning
A float switch sticks every morning and frees itself

inference.explanation: Pumps test at capacity, a sticking float would not match a measured inflow surge, and infiltration does not follow a weekday school schedule. The surge timing and the institution schedule align exactly.

nextClue.prompt: Which next step best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Flow logging at the institution lateral for one week to confirm the surge source and size
A catchment infiltration survey
Float switch replacement as the sole action

nextClue.explanation: Logging the institution lateral confirms the surge size the station must be managed for.

clueText.nc-a: The lateral log shows the surge is most of the station inflow in that hour, matching alarm days.
clueText.nc-b: Floats were observed cycling normally during an alarm event.
clueText.nc-c: Infiltration does not turn off on weekends, so a survey does not fit the pattern.
